title: the Devi Mahatmya (13 chapters, read whole)
hook: the book ends where it began: the king and the merchant go to a riverbank, and the goddess asks what each one wants

segments.voice: Yesterday in the Devi Mahatmya, Shumbha said the goddess fought with borrowed strength, and she answered: I am alone here in the world.
screen: `THE DEVI MAHATMYA.` · `I AM ALONE HERE IN THE WORLD.`

segments.voice: Remember the forest? A king who'd lost his kingdom, a merchant thrown out by his own family, both asking a sage why knowing doesn't help. Year four began with them. Every story since, the sleeping Vishnu, the buffalo, Kali, Raktabija, Shumbha, has been the sage's answer to the king's question: who is this goddess? Now the battles are done. One more hymn, one more promise, and then the book walks back into the forest, to the two men who were listening the whole time.
screen: `BACK TO THE FOREST.` → `EVERY STORY WAS AN ANSWER.` → `WHAT WILL THEY DO WITH IT?`

segments.voice: In the eleventh chapter, after Shumbha falls, the gods praise her once more, calling her Narayani, and ask her to be gracious to the whole world. Her promise is bigger than before. In paraphrase: whenever trouble rises from the demons, I will come down and destroy the enemy. She even names future appearances. In one, during a terrible drought, she will feed the world with plants grown from her own body, and be called Shakambhari, she who bears the greens. In the twelfth chapter she tells the gods what hearing this story brings to those who recite and listen. Then the thirteenth, the last. Medhas finishes: this is the goddess I told you of. She draws you into confusion, and she can set you free. Go to her. So the king and the merchant go to a riverbank, make an image of the goddess out of earth, and worship her there a long time, with offerings and their whole attention. She appears and asks each what he wants. The king asks for his kingdom back in this life, and a kingdom that won't be lost in the next. She grants it. The merchant, who couldn't stop worrying about the family that threw him out, asks for something else. In paraphrase: the knowledge that cuts the knot of I and mine. She grants that too. Two men, the same stories, two requests, and the text doesn't rank them. The book that began with two worries ends with two answers.
screen: `THE GODDESS AS NARAYANI.` · `WHENEVER TROUBLE RISES, I WILL COME.` · `AN EARTH IMAGE BY A RIVER.` · `A KINGDOM, AND FREEDOM FROM I AND MINE.` · then, large: `TWO WORRIES, TWO ANSWERS.`

segments.voice: Let the goddess's question sit quietly in you: what do you want? Let the first, practical answer come, the kingdom, and notice it kindly; then wait a little longer for a quieter one underneath, the merchant's kind, without choosing between them. If you pray, bring both before the goddess or God in your own words; if not, let the question rest on the breath.
The Devi Mahatmya. The glory of the goddess, read whole: a book that begins with two men in a forest who can't let go, and ends with each of them asking her for what he wants.
Your line: the Devi Mahatmya, read whole. She asked each man what he wanted, and granted both. Ten days, one book, read whole.

howItsDone: Some Hindus who recite the whole Devi Mahatmya finish with the thirteenth chapter's boons to the king and the merchant, and the eleventh chapter's hymn to Narayani is also chanted on its own.

original.note: Sanskrit: Nārāyaṇī, a name of the goddess in the gods' hymn of the eleventh chapter.

trapdoor: what you thought: a battle book that ends when the last demon dies.
what it means: the stories were a sage's answer to a king's question; the book ends back in the forest, with two men asking the goddess for two different things.
what a scholar hears: the frame closes in chapter 13: Suratha and Samādhi worship an earthen image, and receive a kingdom and liberating knowledge.

chat.says: So what did the king and the merchant ask the goddess for at the end?

chat.meaning: In chapter thirteen the king asks for his kingdom, here and hereafter; the merchant asks for the knowledge that cuts I and mine. She grants both.

Narayani.meaning: a name the gods praise the goddess by

Devi Mahatmya.meaning: the glory of the goddess, now read whole

recall: right conduct, the right way of living

notes: Last of the ten Devi Mahatmya days; covers chapters 11–13 and closes the frame opened on 1062.

Ch. 11 paraphrased: the gods praise her as Nārāyaṇī (the sarvamaṅgala-māṅgalye verse is in this hymn, not quoted); her promise (itthaṃ yadā yadā bādhā dānavotthā bhaviṣyati / tadā tadāvatīryāhaṃ kariṣyāmy arisaṃkṣayam); Śākambharī during a drought, nourishing the world with life-sustaining vegetables grown from her own body. The text's other named future forms (born of Yashoda, Raktadantika, Shatakshi, Durga, Bhima, Bhramari) are not named. Confirm.

Ch. 12 summarized in one sentence. Ch. 13: Medhas's closing words, the riverbank, the earthen image, worship (the text gives a length of time, not spoken), the boons: the king his kingdom in this life and an imperishable one hereafter (and rebirth as Manu Sāvarṇi, not mentioned); the merchant the knowledge that destroys the attachment of 'I' and 'mine' (mamāham iti). Confirm.
Practice draws on the goddess asking each man what he wants; it does not rank the two requests, as the text doesn't. Confirm a Keeper is comfortable with 'the text doesn't rank them'.
